official-statistics.limits: The sources describe US practice; other statistical offices publish their own vintages, adjustments and measures of sampling error.
official-statistics.mechanism: Official estimates come in vintages: an early estimate built on incomplete data is revised as more data arrive, sometimes years later. Many come from samples and carry sampling error: a reported change whose confidence interval includes zero is not statistically different from no change. A change measured in current prices can reflect prices, quantities or both, so real, inflation-adjusted measures are kept apart from nominal ones. Seasonal adjustment removes recurring patterns within the year so that consecutive months or quarters can be compared, and monthly or quarterly figures are often shown at annual rates. Levels and growth rates answer different questions and are compared only like with like.

facts.text: The European Commission presented an EU Framework for Climate Resilience on 27 Oct 2026, with a proposed Climate Resilience Law that sets a common global warming reference trajectory (1.5C by 2030, 2C by 2050, 3C by 2100).

The Commission says one single national strategic plan will replace separate national planning obligations, and it presents new digital tools: the European Climate Viewer, the Navigator of Climate Resilience Tools and the Solutions Explorer.

The Commission estimates climate damage losses of about €200 billion in 2022-2025 (€50 billion a year) and adaptation investment needs of about €70 billion a year, with returns that can exceed 10 times the investment.

A European Heatwave Plan, a Climate Insurance Alliance, a European Water initiative and identification of the 100 most vulnerable territories are to be presented separately; a strategic plan is due in 2028.

Commissioner Hoekstra said only a quarter of catastrophe losses are covered by private insurance, that roughly €30 billion is earmarked for climate resilience in the current MFF, and that many elements will only be delivered in 2027.

The Commission says measures will be funded within the existing budgetary framework, Member States keep flexibility on measures, and the EIB Group plans at least €30 billion for climate resilience by 2030.

facts.text: The ECB's October 2026 bank lending survey reports a further net tightening of credit standards for firms (net 9% of banks) and consumer credit (14%) in Q3 2026, with unchanged standards for housing loans (0%). Higher risk perceptions were the main driver.

Banks reported a net decrease in loan demand in Q3 2026: firms -6%, housing -27% (-15% in Q2), consumer credit -2%. Interest rates were the main driver. For Q4 banks expect housing -36%, consumer credit -14%, firms -1%.

Several banks expect a gradual but sustained rise in loan demand to finance AI digital infrastructure, particularly data centres. Most banks have not yet set specific quantitative criteria for AI-related lending.

Banks' access to retail funding deteriorated further; the ECB says the deterioration, though still moderate, was the largest since the series began in 2011. Banks expect access to funding to deteriorate further. The survey covered 159 banks, with a 100% response rate.
